summary.value: The Sebright is a tiny English bantam created by Sir John Saunders Sebright, who spent years crossing small local birds before presenting it around 1810. It is a true bantam, so there is no large version, and it ranks among the oldest British bantam breeds. Every feather is gold or silver with a crisp black edge, and cocks are hen feathered, lacking the long curved tail plumes of most roosters. Males weigh about 22 ounces and females about 20. Hens lay only 60 to 80 small creamy white eggs a year and seldom go broody. Sebrights are active and spunky and tame easily when handled young, though they fly well and can be hard to catch. They prefer warm climates and dislike cold, damp weather. The breed is kept for shows and ornament, suits 4H projects, and is a poor choice for anyone wanting eggs.
